setup.zh: 正殿里没有神像，只有一口空的石座，四方，四足。石座前立着测灵石，观主玄沉子坐在一旁。轮到你了。
setup.en: No statue in the main hall — only an empty stone seat, square, on four feet. Before it stands the spirit stone; the abbot Xuanchenzi sits beside it. It is your turn.

recap.zh: 测灵石测出了你的灵根；瞿老说「腿稳，心细」，观主说：收，外门。
recap.en: The spirit stone read your roots; Elder Qu said "steady legs, careful heart," and the abbot said: take them — the outer court.

zh: 正殿没有神像，只有一口空的石座。
四方，四足，大得能躺下一个人。
测灵石前，把手放上去——看它亮几种颜色。
en: No statue in the hall — only an empty stone seat.
Square, four-footed, big enough to lie in.
Before the spirit stone: lay your hand on it, and see how many colours it shows.

text.zh: 石座四只脚下各压出一个方方的深坑；座上空空的——原先该坐着一样极重的东西。
text.en: Under each of the seat's four feet the floor is pressed into a deep square pit. The seat is bare; something very heavy must once have sat on it.

text.zh: 石面光溜溜的，正中凹下去一块，是千百只手按出来的。你把手心在衣襟上擦了两擦。
text.en: The stone is worn smooth, a hollow pressed into its middle by a thousand hands. You wipe your palm twice on your coat.

text.zh: 殿门边靠着一把秃扫帚——扫石阶的那个老头也来了，站在柱子后头，谁也不看。
text.en: A worn broom leans by the hall door: the old man who sweeps the steps has come too. He stands behind a pillar and looks at no one.

story.zh:
正殿在山门里头最高的一层台子上。

殿很大，很旧，梁上的彩画褪得只剩了影子。殿里没有神像。别处的道观，正殿里供的是三清，是真武，是土地爷，这里什么都没有供，只在正中间，摆着一口空的石座。那石座四四方方，底下四只脚，大得能躺下一个人，石面上磨得光溜溜的，中间却有一块颜色比别处深，四四方方，像是许多年前，那上头曾经压过一样很重很重的东西。

石座前头，立着一块一人多高的测灵石，灰扑扑的，看不出什么稀奇。

过了三试的孩子，统共一百来个，在殿里排成长长的一队，一个一个上去测灵根。排队的时候，殿里嘀嘀咕咕，有人问这石座是做什么的，为什么不供神仙。一个唱名的执事，四十来岁，生着一张没睡醒的脸，靠在柱子上，听见了，打了个呵欠，道：「每三年都有人问。」

「古时候，天下有九口鼎，大禹铸的。周朝的时候，鼎在周天子那里。后来周朝不行了，鼎就没了——有人说，是沉到了咱们底下这条泗水里。秦始皇统一天下，路过这里，斋戒了，祷告了，发了一千个人下水去捞。」

一个孩子问：「捞着了没有？」

执事道：「没有。」

又一个孩子问：「一千个人，捞一口锅，都捞不着？」

执事看了那孩子一眼，道：「那不是锅。」顿了一顿，又道：「……好吧，也算是锅。」

「本观开山的祖师，就在这山上结了庐，守着这条河，说鼎是有灵的，德到了，它自己会浮起来。这石座，就是给它留的。」执事又打了个呵欠，「留了三百年了。」

那孩子又问：「那它浮起来了没有？」

执事道：「你看这上头，有鼎么？」

殿里的孩子们都笑了。小满没有笑。他看着那口空石座中间，那块四四方方、颜色比别处深的印子，心想：一千个人，下一条河，捞一口锅。他想起吴婆婆说，有一个皇帝，铸了一口锅，一条龙来接他上天；又想起那管二试的老执事说，大禹铸了九口，一州一口。他胸口那块木牌，这时候不烫，也不暖，就那么贴着他的心口，一下一下，跟着他的心跳。

观主玄沉子坐在石座旁边一张蒲团上，一身灰袍，面目温和，看上去比山下镇上卖布的掌柜还要和气几分。他不大说话，孩子们一个一个上去把手放在测灵石上，他便看一眼石头，再看一眼孩子，点一点头。有时候他的眼睛会从测灵石上移开，往旁边那口空石座上落一落，落一下，又收回来，谁也没有留意。

牛棚里那个瘦孩子也在队里，排在小满前头，正是孙二狗。

小满瞧见他，倒吃了一惊。孙二狗回过头来，冲他咧了咧嘴，小声道：「三步一口气。」小满道：「你也上来了？」孙二狗道：「香剩最后一点点的时候上来的。脚底下踩着最后一级，香灰就掉了。」他顿了一顿，又道：「那半张饼，顶用。」

轮到孙二狗了。他把手放上去，测灵石半天没有动静，好一会儿，才极勉强地透出一点光来，四种颜色，淡得像是隔着一层窗户纸。唱名的执事还当是石头坏了，伸手在石头上拍了两下，那光也不见亮。执事叹了口气，念道：「金、木、火、土，四灵根，色极淡。下下之资。」顿了一顿，又问：「叫什么？」那瘦孩子道：「……孙二狗。」殿里有人笑。孙二狗没有笑，也没有低头，只把那个比他身子还大的包袱，往背上紧了紧。

小满后来才知道，那包袱里装的，是他娘给他缝的三双鞋，一双比一双大，是预备着他在山上一年一年地长个子的。

排在小满前面第三个的，是一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘。

她把手放上去，测灵石亮起三种颜色，青、黑、黄，亮得刺眼。执事一下子睁开了没睡醒的眼睛，念道：「木、水、土，三灵根——真灵根。中上之资。」

殿里又是一阵惊叹。小满踮起脚，想看看是谁，人太多，前头的人头挡着，他只看见一截小辫子一晃，就给人群挡住了。

红鼻头。小辫子。小本子。

小满心里咯噔一下：不会吧？

可石坳村的姑娘，怎么会跑到这儿来？阿禾她娘，连村口那棵老槐树都不让她过。他摇了摇头，心想一定是看错了。这天底下红鼻头的姑娘多了，冻一冻，谁的鼻头不红。

马小宝排在小满前头第一个。他的裤子已经换过了，换了一条更绸的。他把手往测灵石上一拍，拍得「啪」的一声，好像拍的是自家的桌子。测灵石亮了，三种颜色，金、火、土，却灰扑扑的，像蒙了一层灰。执事念道：「金、火、土，三灵根，色浊。中下之资。」

马小宝的脸色，由红变白，由白变青。他身后一个家丁凑到执事跟前，低声说了句什么，把那封盖着县衙大印的荐书又亮了一亮。执事看看荐书，看看玄沉子。玄沉子没有说话。执事便在名册上写了个字。

轮到小满了。

他往前走的时候，心里忽然打了一个突：这块石头，测的是人身上的灵气。那他胸口那块木牌里睡着的那个，算不算他身上的？要是这石头一亮，亮出一道银光来，亮出一条尾巴来，满殿的人都瞧见了——

「藏。在你打得过所有人之前，不许让任何人知道本王。」

小满的手心里，登时出了一层冷汗。他隔着衣裳，把那块木牌往怀里按了按，按得紧紧的，心里说：银月，你可千万睡沉一点。

木牌凉凉的，一动不动，凉得像一块真正的木头。小满后来才明白，那不是她睡得沉，是她把自己藏起来了，藏得比他还好。

他走上前去，把手放在测灵石上。那石头凉凉的，比他胸口那块木牌还凉。
story.en:
The main hall stood on the highest terrace inside the gate.

The hall was very large and very old, the paintings on the beams faded to shadows. There was no image in it. Other temples' main halls held the Three Pure Ones, the True Warrior, the Earth God; here nothing was enshrined; only in the very centre stood an empty stone stand. It was square, four legs under it, big enough for a person to lie on, its top worn smooth — but in the middle a patch was darker than the rest, square, as though many years ago something very, very heavy had once stood on it.

In front of the stand stood a spirit-testing stone taller than a man, dusty grey, nothing remarkable to look at.

The children who'd passed the third trial, a hundred or so all told, lined up in a long queue in the hall to go up one by one and have their roots tested. Queuing, they muttered; someone asked what the stone stand was for and why no immortal was enshrined. A steward who called the names, forty-odd, with a face that hadn't woken up, leaning on a pillar, heard, yawned, and said: "Someone asks every three years."

"In ancient times there were nine *ding* under heaven, cast by Yu the Great. In the Zhou dynasty the *ding* were with the Son of Heaven. Later the Zhou declined, and the *ding* were lost — some say they sank into this very Si River below us. When the First Emperor of Qin unified the world he passed through here, fasted, prayed, and sent a thousand men into the water to dredge for them."

A child asked: "Did they find them?"

The steward said, "No."

Another asked: "A thousand men dredging for one pot, and they couldn't find it?"

The steward looked at that child. "It's not a pot." A pause. "…Well, all right, it's a pot of sorts."

"The founder of this temple built a hut on this mountain and kept watch over the river; he said the *ding* have spirits — when virtue arrives, they'll rise of themselves. This stand was left for one." The steward yawned again. "Left three hundred years now."

The child asked again: "Has it risen?"

The steward said, "See a *ding* up there?"

The children in the hall all laughed. Xiaoman didn't. He looked at the darker square mark in the middle of the empty stand and thought: a thousand men, down into a river, dredging for a pot. He remembered Granny Wu saying: there was an emperor who cast a pot, and a dragon came to take him to heaven; and the old steward of the second trial saying Yu the Great cast nine, one to a province. The token at his chest, just then, neither burned nor warmed; it just lay against his heart, beat by beat, keeping time with it.

The abbot, Xuanchenzi, sat on a cushion beside the stone stand, in a grey robe, his face gentle, looking even more amiable than the cloth merchant in the town below. He didn't say much; as the children came up one by one and laid their hands on the stone, he looked once at the stone, once at the child, and nodded. Sometimes his eyes left the stone and came to rest on the empty stand beside it, rested a moment, and came back; nobody noticed.

The thin boy from the cowshed was in the queue too, just ahead of Xiaoman: Sun Ergou.

Seeing him, Xiaoman was surprised. Sun Ergou turned back and grinned, and said quietly: "Three steps a breath." Xiaoman said, "You got up too?" Sun Ergou said, "Came up when the incense had just a tiny bit left. My foot landed on the last step and the ash fell." He paused. "That half flatbread — did the trick."

Sun Ergou's turn. He laid his hand on the stone; for a long time it did nothing, then with great reluctance showed a faint light, four colours, pale as if through window paper. The steward thought the stone was broken and slapped it twice; the light didn't brighten. The steward sighed and read out: "Metal, wood, fire, earth — four roots, very pale. The lowest of the low." A pause. "Name?" The thin boy said: "…Sun Ergou." Someone in the hall laughed. Sun Ergou didn't laugh, and didn't hang his head either; he only hitched the bundle bigger than himself tighter on his back.

Only later did Xiaoman learn that the bundle held three pairs of shoes his mother had sewn for him, each a size bigger than the last, ready for him to grow year by year on the mountain.

Third in line ahead of Xiaoman was a girl with two little braids.

She laid her hand on it, and the stone lit three colours, green, black, yellow, dazzling. The steward's sleepy eyes flew open. "Wood, water, earth — three roots — a true root. Above the middle."

Another murmur of wonder went round the hall. Xiaoman went up on his toes to see who it was; too many people, heads in front blocking; he saw only the end of a braid flick, and the crowd closed over it.

Red nose. Little braids. Little notebook.

Xiaoman's heart gave a jolt: surely not?

But how would a girl from Shi'ao Village end up here? Ahe's mother wouldn't even let her past the old locust at the village gate. He shook his head: must have seen wrong. There are plenty of red-nosed girls under heaven; freeze anyone a bit and their nose goes red.

Ma Xiaobao was first in line ahead of Xiaoman. His trousers had been changed, for silkier ones. He slapped his hand down on the stone — *smack* — as if slapping his own table. The stone lit: three colours, metal, fire, earth, but greyish, as if under a layer of dust. The steward read: "Metal, fire, earth, three roots, muddy. Below the middle."

Ma Xiaobao's face went from red to white, from white to green. One of his servants leaned to the steward and said something low, and flashed the letter with the county seal again. The steward looked at the letter, at Xuanchenzi. Xuanchenzi said nothing. The steward wrote a character in the register.

Xiaoman's turn.

As he went forward his heart suddenly skipped: this stone tested the spirit-qi in a person. Then the one asleep in the token at his chest — did she count as part of him? If the stone lit, and lit up a silver light, lit up a tail, for the whole hall to see —

"Hide. Until you can beat everyone, no one may know about this king."

A cold sweat broke out on Xiaoman's palms. Through his clothes he pressed the token tight to his chest and said in his heart: Yinyue, you'd better sleep good and deep.

The token was cool, perfectly still, cool as a real piece of wood. Only later did Xiaoman understand: it wasn't that she slept deep; she'd hidden herself — hidden even better than he did.

He went up and laid his hand on the stone. It was cool, cooler than the token at his chest.

label.en: Give your birthday · The root test

exits.means: gives the day they were born, or lets the stone read them — the page card asks it

story.zh:
测灵石亮了——亮得很暗。

金、青、黑、红、黄，五种颜色，一样不少，都有一点，哪一种都不多，哪一种都不亮，你挤着我，我挨着你，灰蒙蒙地搅在一处，像他娘拿家里用剩下的五种碎布头，拼成的一块抹布。{主亮}

殿里静了一静。

然后，有人笑出了声。

笑得最响的，是马小宝。他方才那张青了的脸，这时候又红润了起来，笑得前仰后合，笑得手里的桂花糕渣子掉了一地，一面笑，一面拿手指着那块测灵石，像是指着一个天大的笑话。他这一笑，殿里的孩子们便都笑了，一个传一个，一片一片地笑开去，笑声撞在那褪了色的大梁上，又落下来。

满殿的人，笑的笑，看的看。只有两个人没有笑。一个是蒲团上的玄沉子；另一个，是排在前头、早已测完了的那个扎小辫子的姑娘。她站在人堆后头，低着头，拿炭条在小本子上记了一笔，记得很重，炭条都记断了。

唱名的执事也笑了一笑，拖长了声音念道：「金、木、水、火、土——五行俱全。五行杂灵根。下下之资。」

笑声更大了。

小满站在测灵石跟前，手还放在石头上，没有拿下来。他没有笑，也没有哭。他看着那块抹布一样的石头，心里想的是：五行俱全。什么都有，什么都不多。倒是跟我家一样，四只碗，一只没缺口的也没有了，可四只都还在。

玄沉子没有笑。

他看了看测灵石，又看了看小满。他看小满的时候，比看测灵石的时候长得多，长得小满都有点发毛了，不知道该把手拿下来，还是再放一会儿。

然后玄沉子转过头去，问站在殿门口的一个人：「三试。瞿老以为如何？」

殿里的孩子们这才发现，那扫地的老头不知什么时候也进了殿，拄着扫帚，靠在门框上，身上还沾着林子里的松针。

扫地的老头——瞿老——只说了四个字：「腿稳。心细。」

这四个字，殿里的孩子们谁也没当回事。只有站在殿柱边上的几个老执事，互相看了一眼。瞿老在沉鼎观扫了五十年的台阶，三十年没有收过一个徒弟；这三十年里，他评过的孩子，统共不超过三个，说过的话，每回不超过两个字。

玄沉子点了点头：「收。外门。」

笑声，一下子停了。

马小宝也收了。荐书在，外门。

唱名的执事念他名字的时候，瞿老在门口，拿扫帚把门槛扫了一下，扫得很响。可他只是个扫地的，扫帚响归响，名册上的字，是执事写的。

马小宝从小满身边走过去，压低了声音，道：「沈小满，杂灵根也配进山门？等着。在这山里，我有的是法子收拾你。」

小满道：「小宝哥，裤子干了吗？」

马小宝的脸，一下子变成了他爹的那种颜色——先是红，再是紫，再是黑，最后是一种说不出的颜色，蒙山上的人管那颜色叫「完了」色。
story.en:
The spirit-testing stone lit — very dimly.

Metal, green, black, red, yellow — five colours, not one missing, a little of each, none much, none bright, jostling one another, stirred together grey and murky, like a rag his mother had stitched from five kinds of leftover scraps. {主亮}

The hall went still for a moment.

Then someone laughed out loud.

Loudest was Ma Xiaobao. His green face had gone rosy again; he laughed fit to fall over, osmanthus crumbs dropping everywhere, pointing at the stone as at the greatest joke under heaven. With his laughing the children in the hall all laughed, one passing it to the next, laughter spreading patch by patch, bouncing off the faded great beam and falling back down.

Of all the hall, laughing or looking, only two did not laugh. One was Xuanchenzi on his cushion; the other was the girl with the braids, long since tested, standing at the back of the crowd with her head down, writing something in her notebook with the charcoal — writing so hard the charcoal broke.

The steward smiled too, and drew it out as he read: "Metal, wood, water, fire, earth — all five elements. A mixed five-element root. The lowest of the low."

The laughter grew louder.

Xiaoman stood before the stone, his hand still on it, not taking it away. He didn't laugh, and didn't cry. He looked at the rag of a stone and thought: all five elements. Everything there, nothing much of anything. Just like his home — four bowls, and not one without a chip now, but all four still there.

Xuanchenzi didn't laugh.

He looked at the stone, then at Xiaoman. He looked at Xiaoman much longer than at the stone, so long Xiaoman began to feel uneasy, not knowing whether to take his hand away or leave it a while longer.

Then Xuanchenzi turned and asked someone standing at the hall door: "The third trial. What does Elder Qu think?"

Only then did the children notice that the old sweeper had come into the hall at some point, leaning on his broom against the door frame, pine needles from the forest still on him.

The old sweeper — Elder Qu — said only four words: "Steady legs. Careful heart."

Those four words, none of the children in the hall took any notice of. Only a few old stewards standing by the pillars exchanged a look. Elder Qu had swept the steps of Chending Temple fifty years, and in thirty years had not taken a single disciple; in those thirty years the children he'd passed judgement on numbered no more than three, and each time he spoke no more than two words.

Xuanchenzi nodded. "Accepted. Outer court."

The laughter stopped at once.

Ma Xiaobao was accepted too. The letter held: outer court.

As the steward called his name, Elder Qu at the door swept the threshold once with his broom, very loudly. But he was only a sweeper; broom as loud as you like, the characters in the register were the steward's to write.

Ma Xiaobao walked past Xiaoman and said low: "Shen Xiaoman, a mixed root, fit to come through the temple gate? You wait. On this mountain I've got ways of fixing you."

Xiaoman said, "Xiaobao-ge, are your trousers dry yet?"

Ma Xiaobao's face at once turned his father's colour — first red, then purple, then black, and last a colour there's no word for, which the people of Mount Meng called "done for".
